name: Safety and Health in Agriculture Convention (C184)
provisions: National OSH policy for agriculture; risk assessment for machinery, chemicals, animal handling and confined spaces; 18 as minimum age for hazardous farm work; equal protection for temporary and seasonal workers; special measures for women around maternity.
drivers: Agriculture ranked with mining and construction as the most dangerous sectors, with ILO estimates of about 170,000 farmworker deaths a year; many national OSH laws and C155 itself allowed agriculture to be excluded; pesticide-poisoning evidence from the 1990s; sustained pressure from the IUF food and farm workers' union federation.

name: Labour Inspection (Agriculture) Convention (C129)
provisions: A labor inspection system for agricultural undertakings, optionally extended to tenants, sharecroppers and family members; inspectors' powers of entry and preventive control of new plant and substances.
drivers: The 1947 Labour Inspection Convention (C81) covered only industry and commerce, leaving farms uninspected; mechanisation and agrochemicals of the Green Revolution raised accident rates; ILO push in the 1960s to make standards enforceable in newly independent states. Now one of the four ILO governance (priority) conventions.

name: Rural Workers' Organisations Convention (C141)
provisions: Right of all rural workers, including tenants, sharecroppers and small owner-occupiers, to form organizations of their own choosing; state duty to remove legal and practical obstacles to rural organizing.
drivers: Recognition that C87 and C11 did not reach self-employed and landless rural poor; post-colonial agrarian reform and the ILO World Employment Programme (1969); the 1970s development agenda centred on rural poverty, leading into the 1979 FAO World Conference on Agrarian Reform and Rural Development.

name: Plantations Convention (C110)
provisions: A full labor code for plantations: recruitment and contracts, wages, annual leave, weekly rest, maternity protection, employment injury compensation, freedom of association, labor inspection, housing and medical care.
drivers: Decolonisation and the legacy of indentured and penal-contract labor on tea, rubber, sugar and coffee estates in Asia, Africa and the Caribbean; work of the ILO Committee on Work on Plantations from 1950; newly independent states seeking a single standard for estate labor.

name: Protocol to the Plantations Convention (P110)
provisions: Lets ratifying states narrow C110's definition of 'plantation' by size and exclude smaller holdings.
drivers: Very low ratification of C110 and changes in estate structure (smallholder outgrower schemes); the ILO sought flexibility to keep the convention ratifiable.

name: Right of Association (Agriculture) Convention (C11)
provisions: Agricultural workers must have the same rights of association and combination as industrial workers; restrictive laws must be repealed.
drivers: Post-First World War rural labor unrest and the growth of farm unions in Italy, Spain and Central Europe; France contested ILO competence over agriculture, which the Permanent Court of International Justice upheld in Advisory Opinions Nos. 2 and 3 (1922).

name: Minimum Wage Fixing Machinery (Agriculture) Convention (C99)
provisions: Machinery to fix minimum wages for agricultural workers, with partial payment in kind allowed only if appropriate and fairly valued.
drivers: The 1928 Minimum Wage-Fixing Machinery Convention (C26) excluded agriculture; post-war reconstruction and very low farm wages, often paid in kind; agricultural wage boards already in Britain and the Commonwealth served as models.

name: Workmen's Compensation (Agriculture) Convention (C12)
provisions: Extends workers' compensation laws for work injuries to all agricultural wage earners. Treated as outdated; later social security conventions (C121, 1964) cover the ground.
drivers: Early compensation laws covered factories and mines and left farm hands out; the 1921 ILC session was devoted largely to agriculture after the competence dispute.

name: Minimum Age (Agriculture) Convention (C10)
provisions: No employment of children under 14 in agriculture during school hours. Superseded by C138: ratifying C138 for agriculture denounces C10.
drivers: Widespread use of children in European harvests at the cost of schooling; the post-1919 drive for compulsory education.

name: Holidays with Pay (Agriculture) Convention (C101)
provisions: Annual paid holidays for agricultural workers after continuous service. Outdated; the 1970 Holidays with Pay Convention (C132) covers all sectors.
drivers: The 1936 Holidays with Pay Convention (C52) excluded agriculture; post-war welfare-state expansion.

name: Sickness Insurance (Agriculture) Convention (C25)
provisions: Compulsory sickness insurance for agricultural workers. Outdated; replaced by the Medical Care and Sickness Benefits Convention (C130, 1969).
drivers: Spread of Bismarck-style social insurance in the 1920s, which typically started with industry; adopted alongside the industrial sickness convention C24.

name: Minimum Age Convention (C138)
provisions: General minimum age of 15 (14 for developing states), 18 for hazardous work. Art. 5(3): plantations and commercial agriculture must always be covered; family and small holdings producing for local consumption may be excluded.
drivers: Consolidating ten sectoral minimum-age conventions, including C10 for agriculture, into one; the UN Second Development Decade. Fundamental convention since 1998.

name: Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention (C182)
provisions: Immediate action against hazardous child labor, which national lists typically define to include pesticide handling, heavy loads and machinery. Agriculture accounts for about 70% of child labor worldwide.
drivers: Evidence from the ILO's IPEC program (from 1992); the 1998 Global March Against Child Labour; the trade-and-labor 'social clause' debate after the 1996 WTO Singapore Ministerial. The first ILO convention to reach universal ratification (2020).

name: Forced Labour Convention (C29)
provisions: Suppression of forced or compulsory labor. Applied by the ILO supervisory bodies to debt bondage on farms, bonded harvest labor and coerced migrant crews.
drivers: Colonial forced labor for plantations, porterage and public works in Africa and Asia; League of Nations work leading to the 1926 Slavery Convention.

name: Protocol of 2014 to the Forced Labour Convention (P29)
provisions: Prevention, victim protection and access to remedy; protection against abusive and fraudulent recruitment, highly relevant to migrant harvest crews.
drivers: The ILO's 2012 estimate of 21 million people in forced labor, concentrated in agriculture, fishing, construction and domestic work; C29 had nothing on prevention or remedies; the growth of labor trafficking and recruitment-debt schemes.

name: Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention (C169)
provisions: Art. 20: special protection for Indigenous workers, explicitly including seasonal, casual and migrant agricultural workers and those recruited by labor contractors; protection from bonded labor and pesticide exposure.
drivers: Revision of the assimilationist C107 (1957); the rise of Indigenous movements and the UN Working Group on Indigenous Populations (1982); documented abuse of Indigenous seasonal workers on Latin American estates.

name: Chemicals Convention (C170)
provisions: Classification, labeling, safety data sheets and exposure control for hazardous chemicals at work, covering pesticide handling on farms.
drivers: The 1984 Bhopal pesticide plant disaster; growing pesticide-poisoning data among farmworkers in developing countries; gaps between export and use controls.

name: Private Employment Agencies Convention (C181)
provisions: No recruitment fees charged to workers; protection of workers placed by agencies and contractors, the dominant hiring channel for seasonal farm crews in many countries.
drivers: Shift from banning fee-charging agencies (C96) to regulating them as labor markets liberalised in the 1990s; abuses in labor-contractor supply chains.

name: Migration for Employment Convention (Revised) (C97)
provisions: Equal treatment of regular migrant workers on pay, organizing and housing; annexes on recruitment and model bilateral agreements that structured guest-worker farm programs.
drivers: Post-war labor migration schemes, including the US–Mexico bracero program (1942–64) and European agricultural recruitment; revision of the 1939 convention that never entered into force.

name: Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise Convention (C87)
provisions: Right of all workers, farmworkers included, to form and join organizations without prior authorization.
drivers: The 1944 Declaration of Philadelphia; referral from the UN Economic and Social Council in 1947; early Cold War contest over free versus state-controlled unions.

name: Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining Convention (C98)
provisions: Protection against anti-union discrimination and promotion of collective bargaining, including for farm and plantation workers.
drivers: Companion to C87 to cover the employer–worker relationship; post-war industrial relations models.

name: Equal Remuneration Convention (C100)
provisions: Equal pay for work of equal value, relevant to piece-rate and task-based pay gaps between women and men in harvest work.
drivers: Post-war entry of women into paid work; the equal pay principle in the ILO Constitution (1919) and Declaration of Philadelphia.

name: Abolition of Forced Labour Convention (C105)
provisions: Bans forced labor as a method of mobilising labor for economic development, as political coercion, or as labor discipline.
drivers: Cold War-era inquiries into labor camps and forced labor for economic development, including collectivised agriculture; the 1953 UN–ILO Ad Hoc Committee on Forced Labour.

name: Discrimination (Employment and Occupation) Convention (C111)
provisions: Non-discrimination on grounds including race, sex and national extraction, relevant to ethnically segmented farm labor.
drivers: Decolonisation, apartheid and the civil rights movement.

name: Occupational Safety and Health Convention (C155)
provisions: National OSH policy for all branches. Art. 1(2) lets states exclude particular branches, which is how agriculture was often left out. Fundamental since 2022.
drivers: Shift from hazard-by-hazard rules to a systems approach in the 1970s (UK Robens Report 1972); added to the fundamental principles after the COVID-19 pandemic.

name: Promotional Framework for Occupational Safety and Health Convention (C187)
provisions: National OSH system and program, which ILO guidance expects to cover agriculture as a priority sector.
drivers: The ILO 2003 Global Strategy on OSH; low ratification of C155 led to a promotional instrument. Fundamental since 2022.

name: Violence and Harassment Convention (C190)
provisions: Protection against violence and harassment, including during commuting and in employer-provided housing, both acute risks for women farmworkers.
drivers: The #MeToo movement; documentation of sexual abuse of women farmworkers (for example Human Rights Watch's 'Cultivating Fear', 2012); adopted in the ILO centenary year.

name: Minimum Wage Fixing Convention (C131)
provisions: Minimum wage system covering all groups of wage earners, including agriculture, with wages that take account of workers' and families' needs.
drivers: Developing countries found C26 and C99 ill-suited to their needs; the UN Second Development Decade.

name: Migrant Workers (Supplementary Provisions) Convention (C143)
provisions: Suppression of clandestine migration and trafficking; basic rights of all migrants, including irregular ones; equal opportunity for regular migrants.
drivers: Labor-recruitment stops in Europe after the 1973 oil shock and the growth of irregular migration; trafficking of African workers to Europe raised at ECOSOC in the early 1970s.

name: Social Security (Minimum Standards) Convention (C102)
provisions: Minimum standards for nine branches of social security; states may count coverage by worker category, which in practice often left farmworkers outside.
drivers: The 1942 Beveridge Report and the post-war welfare state; the Philadelphia Declaration's call to extend social security.

name: International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
provisions: Rights to work (Art. 6), just and favorable conditions including fair wages and safe work (Art. 7), trade unions (Art. 8), social security (Art. 9) and food (Art. 11). The Committee has applied Art. 7 directly to agricultural workers.
drivers: Codifying the 1948 Universal Declaration; the Cold War split of the draft covenant into two treaties, with economic and social rights championed by socialist and newly independent states.

name: International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families
provisions: Rights of all migrant workers, regular or not; Art. 59 gives seasonal workers specific protections. Ratified mainly by origin states; few destination states.
drivers: An initiative led by Mexico and Morocco in 1979; low ratification of ILO migrant conventions; ECOSOC concern from 1972 over trafficking of African workers into Europe.

name: Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women
provisions: Art. 14: rights of rural women to agricultural credit, equal treatment in land and agrarian reform, social security, training and organizing in self-help groups and cooperatives.
drivers: The UN Decade for Women (1976–85) and the 1975 Mexico City World Conference; recognition that rural women did most farm work without legal recognition.

name: Supplementary Convention on the Abolition of Slavery, the Slave Trade, and Institutions and Practices Similar to Slavery
provisions: Abolishes debt bondage and serfdom, which it defines as being bound to live and labor on land belonging to another, a definition drawn from agrarian tenancy.
drivers: The 1951 UN Ad Hoc Committee on Slavery reported that debt bondage and serfdom persisted in agrarian economies; it extends the 1926 Convention to practices similar to slavery.

name: Slavery Convention
provisions: Suppression of slavery and the slave trade; Art. 5 requires states to prevent compulsory labor from developing into conditions analogous to slavery.
drivers: The League of Nations Temporary Slavery Commission (1924); reports of forced labor in colonial plantations and concessions.

name: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
provisions: Prohibition of slavery, servitude and forced labor (Art. 8); freedom of association including trade unions (Art. 22).
drivers: Codifying the 1948 Universal Declaration; Cold War split from the economic and social covenant.

name: Convention on the Rights of the Child
provisions: Art. 32: protection from economic exploitation and hazardous work that interferes with education; the main human-rights hook for child labor in family agriculture.
drivers: The 1979 International Year of the Child and a Polish draft from 1978; almost universal ratification.

name: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons (Palermo Protocol)
provisions: Defines trafficking to include forced labor, criminalizes it and sets victim-protection duties; used against trafficking into farm work.
drivers: The end of the Cold War and growth of transnational organized crime; the 1990s focus on sex trafficking that came to include labor trafficking.

name: Rotterdam Convention on Prior Informed Consent for Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides
provisions: Trade control. Exporting states need importers' consent for listed pesticides, and developing states can list severely hazardous pesticide formulations that poison users in the field.
drivers: Exports of pesticides banned in the producing state; it turned the voluntary prior-informed-consent procedure of the FAO Code and UNEP London Guidelines (1989) into a treaty.

name: EU CAP Strategic Plans Regulation: social conditionality
provisions: Cuts direct payments to farm beneficiaries found in breach of EU rules on transparent working conditions, OSH and work equipment. Mandatory from 2025 (voluntary from 2023).
drivers: COVID-19 exposed the living and working conditions of seasonal harvest workers in Germany, Spain and Italy; campaigns by the European Parliament, EFFAT and NGOs; Italian caporalato cases.

name: EU Seasonal Workers Directive
provisions: Admission rules and equal treatment for third-country seasonal workers (mostly in agriculture and tourism): maximum stays, adequate accommodation, protection against excessive rent deductions, complaint mechanisms. Date shown in force is the transposition deadline.
drivers: Labor shortages in EU harvests; documented exploitation of irregular farm migrants; part of the 2005 EU Policy Plan on Legal Migration.

name: Revised European Social Charter
provisions: Rights to just conditions, safe work, fair pay, organizing and bargaining, with a collective complaints procedure that has been used on agricultural workers' conditions. Replaces for its parties the 1961 Charter (ETS No. 35, in force 1965).
drivers: Updating the 1961 Charter after the end of the Cold War, as Central and Eastern European states joined the Council of Europe.

name: Additional Protocol to the American Convention on Human Rights (Protocol of San Salvador)
provisions: Right to work (Art. 6), just and equitable conditions including safety and limits on hours (Art. 7), and trade union rights (Art. 8).
drivers: The 1969 American Convention left economic and social rights to a later protocol; return to democracy across Latin America in the 1980s.

name: Protocol on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol)
citation: AU Protocol to the African Charter
provisions: Economic and social welfare rights (Art. 13), women's right to food security and access to land and agricultural inputs (Art. 15), and to sustainable development (Art. 19).
drivers: Gaps in the African Charter on women's rights; the 1995 Beijing Platform for Action; African women's movements.

name: African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
provisions: Art. 15: right to work under equitable and satisfactory conditions and equal pay for equal work.
drivers: Decolonisation and the OAU's move to an African human-rights system after abuses under several regimes in the 1970s.

name: European Convention on Human Rights, Art. 4
provisions: Prohibits slavery, servitude and forced labor, with positive duties on states to investigate and protect.
drivers: Post-war European project and early Cold War; the Council of Europe's founding instrument.

name: EU Employer Sanctions Directive
provisions: Sanctions on employers of irregular migrants, back-pay rights and complaint channels; inspections targeted at high-risk sectors, which in member states' practice center on agriculture.
drivers: The 2008 European Pact on Immigration and Asylum; concern that the informal labor market pulls in irregular migrants.

name: EU Forced Labour Regulation
provisions: Bans products made with forced labor from the EU market, including farm commodities such as cotton, tomatoes and cocoa. Not yet applicable.
drivers: Evidence on forced labor in Xinjiang cotton and tomato chains; the US Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (2021); the 2021 State of the Union commitment.

name: EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive
provisions: Duty for large companies to identify and address human-rights harms, including labor abuses in agricultural supply chains. Application dates were deferred and scope was narrowed by the 2025–26 'Omnibus' amendments; check the consolidated text.
drivers: The 2013 Rana Plaza collapse; the UN Guiding Principles; French (2017) and German (2021) national due diligence laws that pushed for EU harmonization.

name: ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work
provisions: All ILO members, by virtue of membership, must respect five principles whether or not they ratified the conventions: freedom of association, no forced labor, no child labor, no discrimination, and (from 2022) a safe and healthy working environment.
drivers: The trade-and-labor 'social clause' fight at the 1996 WTO Singapore Ministerial, which sent labor standards back to the ILO; the 1995 Copenhagen World Summit for Social Development; COVID-19 for the 2022 OSH amendment.

name: Chowdury and Others v. Greece
citation: ECtHR, App. No. 21884/15, judgment of 30 March 2017
provisions: Held that 42 Bangladeshi strawberry pickers in Manolada had been subjected to forced labor and trafficking, and that Greece breached Art. 4 ECHR by failing to prevent it and to punish those responsible. The leading European judgment on farm labor exploitation.
drivers: The 2013 Manolada shooting, in which foremen fired on workers demanding months of unpaid wages, and the acquittal of the employers in the Greek courts.

name: CESCR General Comment No. 23 on just and favorable conditions of work
provisions: Interprets ICESCR Art. 7 and names agricultural workers as a group needing specific protection: inclusion in minimum-wage and OSH laws, protection from pesticides, limits on piece rates, and decent housing.
drivers: Persistent exclusions of agricultural and domestic workers from labor law found in state reports; the post-2008 crisis rise of informal work.

name: CEDAW General Recommendation No. 34 on the rights of rural women
provisions: Interprets CEDAW Art. 14: rural women's rights to decent work, social protection, land, and protection from pesticide and agrochemical exposure.
drivers: The first CEDAW recommendation devoted to one article; food-price crises (2007–08) and land grabs that hit rural women hardest; links to the 2030 Agenda.

name: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
provisions: Bans slavery and servitude (Art. 4); rights to work, just pay, trade unions (Art. 23), rest and limits on hours (Art. 24), and an adequate standard of living (Art. 25). Parts are widely treated as customary international law.
drivers: The Second World War and the Holocaust; the founding of the UN; drafting led by the Commission on Human Rights chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt.

name: UN Declaration on the Rights of Peasants and Other People Working in Rural Areas (UNDROP)
provisions: Covers peasants and hired agricultural workers. Art. 13 right to work and freedom from forced labor; Art. 14 safety and health, including a right not to use hazardous substances and to refuse unsafe work; Arts. 9–10 association and participation; Art. 16 decent income.
drivers: Two decades of advocacy by La Via Campesina; the 2007–08 food price crisis and large-scale land acquisitions; a Human Rights Council Advisory Committee study (2012) and an intergovernmental working group led by Bolivia.

name: Safety and Health in Agriculture Recommendation (R192)
provisions: Detailed guidance for C184: health surveillance, chemicals management, machinery standards, animal handling, welfare facilities, and extending protection to self-employed farmers.
drivers: Adopted with C184 to give technical detail; same drivers.

name: Labour Inspection (Agriculture) Recommendation (R133)
provisions: Inspectors' advisory role, training, cooperation with farm organizations, and inspection of living conditions.
drivers: Adopted with C129.

name: Rural Workers' Organisations Recommendation (R149)
provisions: Measures to involve rural workers' organizations in agrarian reform, development planning and rural services.
drivers: Adopted with C141.

name: Plantations Recommendation (R110)
provisions: Guidance on recruitment, wages, housing and welfare on plantations.
drivers: Adopted with C110.

name: Tenants and Share-croppers Recommendation (R132)
provisions: Fair rents, security of tenure, compensation for improvements and organization for tenants and sharecroppers.
drivers: Land-reform debates in Latin America and Asia; exploitative sharecropping arrangements.

name: ILO Code of Practice on Safety and Health in Agriculture
citation: ILO, adopted by a Meeting of Experts, October 2010 (published 2011)
provisions: Practical rules on tractors, machinery, chemicals, biological hazards, ergonomics, livestock, heat and welfare facilities. Not binding, but used by inspectors and auditors.
drivers: Low ratification of C184 and demand for an operational tool for national programs.

name: OECD-FAO Guidance for Responsible Agricultural Supply Chains
citation: OECD/FAO (2016), with an OECD Council Recommendation
provisions: Due diligence framework for agribusiness, including a model enterprise policy on labor rights, OSH, child and forced labor.
drivers: The 2011 update of the OECD Guidelines; the food-price crisis and investor attention to land and labor risks in agriculture.

name: Committee on World Food Security Principles for Responsible Investment in Agriculture and Food Systems (CFS-RAI)
provisions: Principle 2: investment should create decent work for agricultural workers, respect core labor standards and OSH.
drivers: The 2008–12 wave of large-scale farmland acquisitions; the G8 and World Bank 'PRAI' principles, which civil society rejected, prompting an inclusive CFS process.

name: FAO/WHO International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management
provisions: Duties of governments and industry on pesticide registration, labeling, protective equipment and avoiding highly hazardous pesticides where workers cannot use them safely.
drivers: Exports of banned pesticides to developing countries; the 1984 Bhopal disaster; campaigning by the Pesticide Action Network, founded 1982.

name: Worst Forms of Child Labour Recommendation (R190)
provisions: Lists factors for defining hazardous child labor, including dangerous machinery, hazardous substances, heavy loads, and long hours, all typical of farm work.
drivers: Adopted with C182.

name: Transition from the Informal to the Formal Economy Recommendation (R204)
provisions: Strategy to extend labor and social protection to informal workers, the majority of agricultural workers worldwide.
drivers: Informality persisted after the 2008 crisis at about 60% of global employment and over 90% in agriculture.

name: ILO General Principles and Operational Guidelines for Fair Recruitment
citation: ILO, Meeting of Experts 2016; definition of recruitment fees 2018
provisions: No recruitment fees or related costs charged to workers; transparent contracts; regulation of labor intermediaries.
drivers: The ILO Fair Recruitment Initiative (2014); recruitment debt behind forced labor in migrant farm and fishing work.

name: UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
provisions: Art. 17: Indigenous individuals' right to labor rights, and protection of Indigenous children from exploitative work.
drivers: More than twenty years of drafting since the 1982 Working Group; Indigenous land and labor claims.

name: Forced Labour (Supplementary Measures) Recommendation (R203)
provisions: Guidance on prevention, labor inspection in high-risk sectors, victim identification and remedies.
drivers: Adopted with P29.

name: Social Protection Floors Recommendation (R202)
provisions: Basic income security and health care for all, including informal and seasonal farmworkers excluded from contributory schemes.
drivers: The 2008 financial crisis; the UN Social Protection Floor Initiative (2009) led by Michelle Bachelet.

name: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
provisions: The state duty to protect, the corporate responsibility to respect, and access to remedy, applied by agribusiness and food retailers to supply chains.
drivers: Failure of the 2003 UN Draft Norms; the six-year mandate of Special Representative John Ruggie (2005–11).

name: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct
provisions: Employment and industrial relations chapter, risk-based due diligence and National Contact Points that handle complaints, including from plantation workers.
drivers: The 1970s debate over multinationals (the UN Code of Conduct talks); updated in 2000, 2011 and 2023.

name: ILO Tripartite Declaration of Principles concerning Multinational Enterprises and Social Policy
citation: ILO Governing Body, 1977; latest revision 2017, amended 2022
provisions: Guidance to multinationals and governments on employment, wages, OSH and industrial relations, including in plantation and agro-processing operations.
drivers: The 1970s call for a New International Economic Order and scrutiny of multinationals in the Global South.

name: Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration
provisions: Objective 6: fair and ethical recruitment and decent work; regular pathways including seasonal labor schemes.
drivers: The 2015–16 migration crisis in Europe and the 2016 New York Declaration.

name: 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (SDG Targets 8.7, 8.8, 2.3)
provisions: Ending forced and child labor (8.7), safe and secure work for all including migrants (8.8), and doubling small-scale food producers' incomes (2.3).
drivers: Successor to the Millennium Development Goals, which lacked labor targets.

name: Fair Food Program
citation: Coalition of Immokalee Workers; Fair Food Standards Council
provisions: Worker-written code of conduct for US tomato and other produce farms, with independent audits, a 24-hour complaint line and market consequences for growers. Enforced through legally binding agreements with buyers such as fast-food and supermarket chains.
drivers: US federal forced-labor prosecutions in Florida tomato fields in the late 1990s and 2000s; campaigns by the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, which won its first buyer agreement in 2005.

name: Rainforest Alliance Sustainable Agriculture Standard
provisions: Farm and supply-chain requirements on wages (living-wage assessment), child and forced labor 'assess and address' systems, OSH and grievance mechanisms.
drivers: The 2018 merger of Rainforest Alliance and UTZ; criticism that audit-only models missed hidden child labor in cocoa.

name: Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil Principles and Criteria
provisions: Labor rights on palm plantations: no recruitment fees, no passport retention, living wage, freedom of association, OSH.
drivers: Deforestation and labor-abuse campaigns against palm oil in Indonesia and Malaysia from the early 2000s.

name: Fairtrade Standard for Hired Labour
provisions: Requirements on wages, freedom of association, OSH and a Fairtrade Premium managed by workers on certified plantations.
drivers: The 1989 collapse of the International Coffee Agreement and the fair-trade movement's turn to labeling.

name: Bonsucro Production Standard
provisions: Labor rights and OSH for sugarcane cutting and milling, including heat-stress protection.
drivers: Biofuel demand and scrutiny of sugarcane labor, including deaths from heat stress among cane cutters in Brazil and Central America.

name: Ethical Trading Initiative Base Code
provisions: Nine labor principles based on ILO standards, applied by UK retailers to fresh produce suppliers.
drivers: UK supermarket and apparel sourcing scandals of the 1990s; New Labour's support for ethical trade.

name: SA8000 Standard
provisions: Auditable workplace standard based on ILO conventions, used on some farms and plantations.
drivers: Mid-1990s sweatshop scandals and demand for an auditable social standard comparable to ISO 9001.

name: Fair Labor Standards Act
citation: 29 U.S.C. § 201 et seq.; farm exemptions at § 213(a)(6), (b)(12)
provisions: Federal minimum wage and overtime. Farmworkers were excluded entirely until the 1966 amendments brought larger farms under the minimum wage; agricultural workers remain exempt from federal overtime, and small farms from the minimum wage.
drivers: New Deal labor reform; Southern congressional votes were secured by excluding agricultural and domestic work, sectors then dominated by Black workers.

name: National Labor Relations Act
provisions: Federal right to organize and bargain, with 'agricultural laborers' expressly excluded from the definition of employee, so farmworkers have no federal protection for organizing.
drivers: Same New Deal bargain with Southern Democrats; growers' opposition to farm unions.

name: Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act (MSPA)
provisions: Registration of farm labor contractors; written disclosure of pay and conditions at recruitment; housing and transport safety standards; a private right of action for workers.
drivers: Weak enforcement of the Farm Labor Contractor Registration Act (1963); decades of exposure of migrant conditions since the 1960 documentary 'Harvest of Shame'.

name: H-2A temporary agricultural worker program
citation: Immigration Reform and Control Act 1986; 8 U.S.C. § 1188; 20 C.F.R. Part 655 Subpart B
provisions: Visas for foreign seasonal farmworkers, conditioned on employer-paid housing and transport, an Adverse Effect Wage Rate and a three-quarters work guarantee.
drivers: IRCA's settlement between employer sanctions, legalisation and grower demand for labor; the earlier H-2 program dating back to the end of the bracero era.

name: EPA Agricultural Worker Protection Standard
provisions: Pesticide safety training, restricted-entry intervals after spraying, decontamination supplies and emergency assistance; the 2015 revision set a minimum age of 18 for pesticide handlers.
drivers: Pesticide-poisoning incidents among field workers and litigation by farmworker organizations; the 2015 revision followed evidence of poor training and child exposure.

name: California Agricultural Labor Relations Act
provisions: State-level right of farmworkers to organize and bargain, with secret-ballot elections and an Agricultural Labor Relations Board; filled the gap left by the NLRA exclusion.
drivers: The United Farm Workers' grape strikes and consumer boycotts (1965–70s) led by César Chávez and Dolores Huerta; Governor Jerry Brown's push for labor peace in the fields.

name: Gangmasters (Licensing) Act 2004
provisions: Compulsory licensing of labor providers in agriculture, horticulture and shellfish gathering; criminal offenses for unlicensed operation and for using unlicensed gangmasters. Enforced by the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority.
drivers: The February 2004 Morecambe Bay disaster, in which at least 21 Chinese cockle pickers drowned; earlier campaigning by unions and retailers.

name: Modern Slavery Act 2015
provisions: Slavery and trafficking offenses, and supply-chain transparency statements for large companies, including food retailers sourcing produce.
drivers: Prominent forced-labor cases in UK agriculture and food processing; Home Office political leadership on modern slavery.

name: Law 199/2016 against caporalato
citation: Legge 29 ottobre 2016, n. 199; Art. 603-bis Codice penale
provisions: Criminalizes illegal labor intermediation (caporalato) and labor exploitation by employers, with confiscation of assets and support for workers; part of a network of quality agricultural work.
drivers: The 2015 death of farmworker Paola Clemente in Apulian vineyards and other heat-related deaths; strikes by migrant tomato and orange pickers since the 2010 Rosarno riots.

name: Rural Labour Law
citation: Lei n.º 5.889, de 8 de junho de 1973
provisions: Labor code for rural workers: contracts, hours, night work, deductions for housing and food. The 1988 Constitution (Art. 7) later equalised rural and urban workers' rights.
drivers: Rural unionism and the 1963 Rural Worker Statute that preceded it; military-era modernisation of agriculture.

name: Penal Code Art. 149 as amended (slave-like labor)
citation: Lei n.º 10.803, de 11 de dezembro de 2003
provisions: Defines 'labor analogous to slavery' to include degrading conditions and exhausting hours, not only restriction of movement. Paired with the Ministry of Labour's 'dirty list' of employers (from 2003).
drivers: Mobile inspection groups since 1995 found thousands of workers in slave-like conditions on cattle ranches and in sugarcane and charcoal; the 2004 Unaí killing of labor inspectors kept pressure high.

name: Constitutional Amendment 81/2014 (confiscation of land used for slave labor)
citation: Emenda Constitucional n.º 81, de 5 de junho de 2014; Constitution Art. 243
provisions: Rural and urban properties where slave labor is found can be expropriated without compensation and allocated to agrarian reform.
drivers: A fifteen-year campaign by the National Commission for the Eradication of Slave Labour; the 2003 case of José Pereira before the Inter-American Commission, which Brazil settled.

name: Federal Labour Law, chapter on field workers
citation: Ley Federal del Trabajo (1970), Título Sexto, Capítulo VIII, Arts. 279–284
provisions: Special rules for agricultural workers: permanence after continuous work, housing, medical care, safe water and transport. Reinforced in the 2012 and 2019 labor reforms.
drivers: Codification of the 1917 Constitution's Art. 123 labor rights; later reforms followed the 2015 San Quintín farmworker strike and USMCA labor commitments.

name: Plantations Labour Act 1951
citation: Act No. 69 of 1951; now consolidated into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020
provisions: Housing, medical care, crèches, drinking water, education and hours on tea, coffee, rubber and cardamom estates. Its provisions now sit in the OSH Code, brought into force with the other labor codes in November 2025.
drivers: Independence-era reform of colonial estate labor; the 1946 Rege Committee report on plantation conditions.

name: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976
provisions: Abolishes bonded labor, extinguishes bonded debts and sets up vigilance committees and rehabilitation. Most bonded laborers identified have been in agriculture and brick kilns.
drivers: The 1975 Twenty-Point Programme under the Emergency (the Act replaced an October 1975 ordinance); research on agrarian debt bondage.

name: Sectoral Determination 13: Farm Worker Sector
citation: Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997; SD 13 (2002, in force March 2003)
provisions: Minimum wages, hours, leave and housing deductions for farmworkers. Farm wages have since been folded into the national minimum wage (2018), set at parity from 2022.
drivers: Post-apartheid extension of labor law to farms after centuries of exclusion; the 2012 De Doorns farmworker strikes forced a sharp increase in the minimum.

name: Extension of Security of Tenure Act (ESTA)
provisions: Protects farm dwellers, many of them current or former farmworkers, against arbitrary eviction from farm housing.
drivers: Mass evictions of farmworkers after 1994; the land reform mandate in Section 25 of the 1996 Constitution.

name: Dunmore v. Ontario (Attorney General)
provisions: Supreme Court held that excluding agricultural workers from Ontario's labor relations statute breached freedom of association under the Charter. Ontario responded with the Agricultural Employees Protection Act 2002, upheld in Ontario v. Fraser (2011 SCC 20).
drivers: Ontario's 1995 repeal of the short-lived law that had extended bargaining rights to farmworkers; litigation by the United Food and Commercial Workers union.

name: Horticulture Award 2020: minimum piece-rate guarantee
provisions: Piece-rate workers in horticulture must earn at least the minimum hourly rate for hours worked.
drivers: The Fair Work Ombudsman's Harvest Trail Inquiry (2018) and evidence of widespread underpayment of backpackers and Pacific seasonal workers; an application by the Australian Workers' Union.

name: Duty of Vigilance Law
provisions: Large French companies must publish and implement a vigilance plan covering human-rights risks in their supply chains, including agricultural sourcing.
drivers: The 2013 Rana Plaza collapse and civil-society campaigns after it.

name: Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG)
provisions: Large companies must run risk management against child labor, forced labor and OSH breaches in their supply chains, with oversight by BAFA; widely applied to cocoa, coffee and fruit imports.
drivers: Failure of the voluntary National Action Plan monitoring (2018–20) to show compliance; Rana Plaza and cocoa child-labor evidence.

name: Ministerial Regulation on Labour Protection in Agricultural Work, B.E. 2557
citation: Thailand, 2014, issued under the Labour Protection Act B.E. 2541
provisions: Sets minimum standards for farm employment, which the Labour Protection Act had largely excluded: wages, working hours, rest, holidays, leave, and a minimum age of 15 for farm work. Coverage of short seasonal work is limited.
drivers: Scrutiny of forced and child labor in Thai agriculture and fisheries, including the US downgrade of Thailand in the 2014 Trafficking in Persons Report.

name: Regulation of Wages (Agricultural Industry) Order
citation: Kenya, Labour Institutions Act 2007; orders revised periodically
provisions: Statutory minimum wages, housing allowance and hours for farmworkers by grade, from field workers to tractor drivers, set on the advice of the Agricultural Wages Council.
drivers: Kenya's plantation economy (tea, flowers, coffee) and bargaining by the Kenya Plantation and Agricultural Workers' Union. The 2007 labor reform replaced the colonial-era wage-fixing law (Cap. 229).

name: Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme
citation: Immigration New Zealand, Operational Manual, RSE instructions
provisions: Lets approved horticulture and viticulture employers hire seasonal workers, mainly from Pacific Island states, for up to seven months a year (nine for Kiribati and Tuvalu). Employers must pay at least the market rate, guarantee minimum hours, provide pastoral care and pay half the return airfare.
drivers: Labor shortages in horticulture and viticulture, and New Zealand's Pacific development policy. Partly modeled on Canada's Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program.
